items.title: Your mitochondria used to be a separate organism
items.claim: Mitochondria have their own DNA, their own ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide independently of the cell. About 2 billion years ago, a free-living alpha-proteobacterium got engulfed by another cell and stayed.
items.prompt: What's the strongest evidence mitochondria were once independent?

options.text: They are smaller than the host cell

Mitochondrial DNA is circular (like a bacterial chromosome), their ribosomes resemble bacterial ribosomes (and are inhibited by antibiotics like chloramphenicol), and their inner membrane has bacteria-like lipid composition

items.reveal_title: Lynn Margulis and the endosymbiotic theory
items.reveal:
Lynn Margulis proposed in 1967 that mitochondria descend from free-living alpha-proteobacteria, and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria. Her paper was rejected fifteen times before being accepted. The orthodoxy disliked the idea of major evolution happening by merger rather than gradual modification.

The evidence accumulated:
- Circular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
- Bacterial-style ribosomes; sensitive to bacterial antibiotics.
- Double membranes (the outer from the host cell, the inner from the bacterium).
- Replication by binary fission, independent of cell division.
- Phylogenetic analysis: mitochondrial genes group with Rickettsia (intracellular alpha-proteobacteria).

All eukaryotes (including animals, plants, fungi) descend from this single ancient merger. Without it, complex life wouldn't exist.
items.why: Evolution is taught as branching divergence. Some of the most important steps came from merger — two organisms becoming one.

items.title: Your lungs have the surface area of half a tennis court
items.claim: Two lungs, about 4 to 6 litres total volume — but the internal surface area where gas exchange happens is 50 to 75 square metres. Achieved by 300 to 500 million alveoli, each a tiny sphere with a thin shared wall to a capillary.
items.prompt: Why is so much surface area needed?

options.text: Diffusion of gases across a membrane scales with surface area and inversely with thickness; meeting the body's O2 demand (~250 ml/min at rest, ~3 L/min at exercise) requires both a huge area and an ultra-thin barrier (~0.5 micrometres)
Extra alveoli are spare in case some collapse

items.reveal:
Rate of diffusion = (surface area * concentration gradient) / (membrane thickness). To maximise O2 uptake, organisms maximise area, maximise gradient (high O2 in air vs low in blood) and minimise thickness.

Alveoli: 0.2-0.5 mm diameter spheres, lined with type I cells (extremely thin), surrounded by capillaries. The blood-air barrier is only 2-3 cells thick — sometimes <0.5 micrometres.

If you flattened all alveoli out, they would cover ~70 square metres — close to a singles tennis court.

Diseases that destroy alveoli (emphysema) reduce gas exchange capacity. Pulmonary fibrosis thickens the barrier. Both cause shortness of breath at exertion.

Total lung capillary blood volume is only ~75 ml at rest, but blood transits in ~0.75 seconds — enough for full equilibration in healthy lungs. At maximal exercise, transit time can drop to 0.25 seconds; in well-trained athletes at altitude, diffusion can become rate-limiting.
items.why: Big surface in small volume seems like a packaging miracle. Evolution solved it with tessellated bubbles — and made breathing possible at human body size.
